appraisal_events.evidence: « c’était pour que vous ne parliez pas de Swann » ; « j’ai failli le nommer... c’est épouvantable » ; « Vous n’avez qu’à dire qu’on remette ces dessins en haut, puisqu’ils vous font penser à Swann. Si vous ne pensez pas à Swann, vous ne parlerez pas de lui. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann's name is treated as an embarrassment to be suppressed in the Guermantes house, and the duc proposes banishing his drawings upstairs as a practical cure for remembering him, which locally erases Swann from the valued social space he once occupied. The narration lets the couple's tactful horror and the duc's furniture-logic expose their callousness rather than endorsing the taboo.

appraisal_events.evidence: « l’envie qui lui avait fait feindre d’ignorer mon article cessait, comme un compresseur se soulève » ; « on ne doit pas parler à ses amis des choses humiliantes qui leur arrivent » ; « Son caractère restait le même, mais son style était devenu moins précieux »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator diagnoses Bloch's silence about the article as envy and then quotes the belated, disguised insult by which Bloch dresses that envy as delicacy, so Bloch's affected disdain is exposed as pettiness. The closing verdict that his character is unchanged while only his style has coarsened seals the diminishment as narrator-endorsed.

status_effects.explanation: Swann is locally excluded to the point of unmentionability: his name must not be spoken and even his drawings are to be removed from the room.
The duc comes off worse through his own remark, which reduces the memory of a dead friend to a problem of hanging pictures elsewhere.
Bloch is clearly diminished: his silence is unmasked as envy and his eventual comment as a self-serving insult delivered under the pretext of friendly tact.

The recognition he wants is withheld: the congratulations come from remote or conventional correspondents, Bloch's judgment arrives as an insult, and the one admiring verdict on his article turns out to have been dreamed.

ambiguities: The passage leaves the net movement for the narrator's article underdetermined: Bloch's envy retroactively confirms it as a « privilège », yet the actual congratulations are cold or anonymous and the only warm admiration (Bergotte's, reported by Mme de Forcheville) is explicitly revealed to be a dream, so the article is at once a real distinction and a deflated one.

The Swann taboo has two possible beneficiaries and therefore two readings: it may be chiefly protective consideration for Gilberte, who no longer wishes her father's name pronounced, or a diminishment of Swann himself; the duchesse's move to soften the narrator's blunder points toward tact, while the duc's reply pushes the scene toward posthumous erasure.
